October, 1994       Page Reply

   PLEASE SEND YOUR TEXTFILE!
Text is accepted in any form for
OUTLETTERS: wordprocessor files
(say which),typed or handwritten
letters. However, PLEASE send us
a textfile if possible so your
letter needn't be typed again!
The easiest for us to edit are
Tasword 2 files with the right
margin set at 32 but a textfile
in ANY format is appreciated!

Please state if there should be
parts of your letter you do not
wish published but we always use
our discretion anyway. Letters
may also be edited for clarity
and length... Please ask if you
welcome direct correspondence
from other OUTLET readers and we
will publish your full address.

From Terry Thomas, QWENT

Dear Ron,

Thanks for your comments in Out-
let No.85. Your information is
very useful. Please thank Brian
for his contribution - I can now
print Clip Art successfully and
have printed out your notes for
further use (It is my way of
teaching my grandsons to use the
computer).

Well, Ron, I have got myself an
Amstrad 1512, 5.25" disk drive;
so, do you publish Outlet on the
5.25"? If so could you please
change my subscription to same.

         Thanks again,
            Terry Thomas

Ron Cavers to Terry Thomas


Dear Terry,

Glad to hear that you can now
print the clip art.

I'm sorry to tell you that you
will not be able to run "OUTLET"
for the PC on your Amstrad 1512
5.25" drive system as it is des-
igned to run on VGA 3.5" systems
(or higher) with HD drive.

              Ron Cavers

From Malcolm Perry,KIDDERMINSTER


Dear Ron and Brian



         +2 TAPE SOCKET

Just to clarify a point that may
cause confusion with the item in
Issue 85 on adding a tape socket
to the +2.The first part as said
relates to the BLACK +2 but the
second part should read GREY +2
(not BLACK as stated). incid-
entally the original letter is
in Issue #75 not 25, I thought 4
years ago seemed a long time! If
error in my original text apol-
ogies to all.


I read with interest the reply
from Francis Miles on my SHOUT-
BURST from a point of view on
the other side of the fence
which in the main confirmed the
point I was making. However in
defence I must comment on the
statement that it seems all
except myself know prices are
set by market forces. Are they?

Obviously market forces have a
say where there is competition
such as dozens of shops in the
High Street all selling similar
items. But take the extreme of
monopoly industries; they have
the market; you use their serv-
ice and pay whatever they, their
accountants, shareholders prof-
its, directors' inflated salary
and so on demand -or go without.

If you decide your local electr-
icity, gas or water company
charges too much, can you go to
the shop next door?

More relevantly, how much choice
do you have to be able to shop
around the High street (or else-
where) for Spectrum or SAM
items?

It is not only the workers and
so on at a firm who lose out if
a firm goes bust. I personally
have "lost out" a number of
times when a firm closes down
after they had the money but
before I received the goods, or
no longer have any guarantee
because the firm no longer
exists.


I personally have seen traders
at shows agreeing prices for
similar items before the public
arrive or one buying up entire
stocks of a "cheap" item from
another and then offer it at a
higher price by opening time.


One trader told me that he was
extremely unpopular because he
refused to raise his prices in
line with others. Good for him
for making a stand, but he might
be forced out as other traders
could decline to attend if he is
allowed to. Customer or market
forces have little or no look
in.



I will finish on an incident
that happened in this area some
years ago. A small dealer was
selling a TV at less than a
large chain store. The large
store under its "if you see it
cheaper we will refund" did just
that.

The chain store then got onto
the manufacturer and told them
if they did not instruct the
small shop to raise their prices
the large company would no
longer deal with that firm.


The firm's interest being in
large turnover rather the odd
one or two a year from a small
business did just that.


The small shop to its credit
told the firm where to go and
transferred to another make;
even so,the chain store had won.

Market forces setting prices?
looked more like blackmail by a
large company to maintain higher
prices to me.

               Malcolm Perry

From E.C. Norfolk, HULL

Dear Ron & Brian,

I received the latest disk and
it worked a treat. I liked the
screen: 'Raiders Of The Lost
Outlet' - one of the best I have
ever seen.

I have recently purchased a 3.5"
external disk drive.[for the +3]
Yes, it came from Chris Box so I
have enclosed a copy of the ins-
tructions.[see summary following
this letter in my reply - Brian]

The drive supplied by Chris Box
is a Sony IBM drive. All worked
well.It was clean, as new - not
like drives at radio rallies.


The leads are easy to assemble -
taking only a few minutes to put
it together.

        Best Regards to
       the Chezron Team,

         Chris Norfolk

Brian Cavers to Chris Norfolk

Thanks, Chris. The info you sent
is so comprehensive it is worth
summarising here for any other
+3 users who might be interested
in adding a 3.5" disk drive with
over 700K storage space.

The kit consists of...

1. The 3.5" drive giving 706K.

2. A ribbon cable (to go in the
   'B' drive socket on the +3)

3. A Y-shaped power adaptor lead
   so the new drive can share
   your existing +3 power unit.

4. A software disk to format,etc


Make sure the +3 is disconnected
from the mains then plug in the
leads and switch back on, put
the new supplied software disk
in the new drive and just enter:
      LOAD "B:FORMAT.BAS"

You then have a menu to FORMAT
or CAT drives A or B or copy any
files from A to B or B to A. You
still can only get a maximum of
64 files on the B drive with the
software provided but BFORMAT in
OUTLET 48 lets you have 128 or
even 256! You can't obviously,
copy a full 700K disk to a 3"
disk but otherwise it all sounds
plain sailing. Read your +3
manual on using the syntax "A:"
and "B:" to access each drive if
you are in doubt.


The complete kit of disk drive,
leads and disk is `43 including
postage or you can add `2 to get
a guaranteed (insured) delivery.
Make out cheques (a postal order
is preferred) to Mrs. Tracey Box
and allow up to two weeks for
delivery. Order from...

           Chris Box
       31 Stanley Street
            Semilong
          Northampton
            NN2 6DD

You might mention you heard it
in OUTLET!

Finally though, please note we
CANNOT produce a +3,3.5" version
of OUTLET - sorry!
                        Brian

From Fred Ridout, SWINDON


Dear Ed's,

I am intending to get a printer
for my 128+2 and I would like to
know if you would advise a
serial or parallel. I was think-
ing of a citizen 120D+ or simi-
lar.

I have a DATEL ELECTRONICS INTER
Printer interface but no info as
to how to use it.Inside it there
is only one IC which is a Z80
PIO I think. It has to have some
OUT pokes to initiate. It has a
parallel plug attached on a
ribbon cable about 1 Metre long.
Any advice would be appreciated.


While on the subject of printers
I have the on-screen memory U2
utility which has block delete,
renumber, and llist to ZX
printer. It prints the llisting
on a ZX printer in 128 mode
without corrupting the 128
sysvars. Is it not possible to
lprint as well, using whatever
code the utility uses?

By the way, regarding the inter-
face, I have had no reply from
DATEL to an inquiry.

        Yours hopefully,

          F. Ridout

Brian Cavers to Fred Ridout

Generally speaking I would reco-
mmend parallel for printers. The
Citizen 120D is parallel but you
can get an interchangeable int-
erface card for serial use so it
might be worth asking about that
when buying. You then have some
reassurance that if you cannot
get the parallel interface work-
ing you should still be able to
get the serial interface.

Does any other reader have the
instructions for the Datel
printer interface?

It may be possible for a machine
code programmer to alter U2 to
LPRINT but it is unlikely to be
easy.

If you really want to LPRINT to
a ZX printer in 128K mode, load
TOGGLER from this issue. Press E
to extract line 9409 then add...

9407 FOR A=23296 TO 23551:
     POKE A+20000,PEEK A:
     NEXT A: GO SUB 9409:RETURN

9408 FOR A=23296 TO 23551:
     POKE A,PEEK (A+20000):
     NEXT A:GO SUB 9409: RETURN

Save it all.MERGE in any program
within which you want to LPRINT.
GOSUB 9407 before and GOSUB 9408
after an LPRINT, eg...

GOSUB 9407:LPRINT xxx:GOSUB 9408

I have not tested it and it will
be slow but should work.

You will appreciate that it is
not really LPRINTing in 128K
mode but is switching briefly
to 48K, LPRINTing, and then
returning to 128K. It is all
invisible with no effect on the
program and you would not even
know it had happened.

The FOR NEXT loops copy the 128K
sysvars to higher memory and
copy them back after printing.An
alternative might be to copy
them to higher memory only once
at the start of the program with
just the first loop (not the GO
SUB) so they only need copying
back AFTER each LPRINT(you still
need a GO SUB 9409 before the
LPRINT to switch to 48K). I do
not know if any problems might
arise though!

If you try this out and find it
really useful - although a bit
slow - let me know and I will
write you a small machine code
routine to copy the memory back
and forth instantly.

                        Brian

From Francis Miles, WELWYN


Dear Ron and Brian,

Your comment on my letter (prod-
uct pricing) in OUTLET 85 made
me think: to a considerable ex-
tent I agree with you but there
is more to be said.

In this country, under the inf-
luence of the media, there is a
strong tendency to make the equ-
ation "profit = greed". There's
some justification for it: there
are greedy people who run com-
panies, milk them of as much
cash as they possibly can for as
long as they can for their own
personal use, and when the sands


have run out liquidate the com-
pany (putting all their employ-
ees on the dole) and retire to
their villa in Switzerland or
the Cayman Islands or wherever
and lead the life of Riley till
they die and go to Hell.

Such people are in a minority:
even in England, though I have
the impression there are more of
them in England (I don't mean
Britain) than anywhere else -
and I have been around a bit.

Mostly people who run businesses
think of profit as a necessary
resource, without which the bus-
iness can't survive. What do
they work for, then, if not per-
sonal profit? Some because they


love their work - the craftsman
making hand-built furniture, and
(I suspect) the Cavers brothers.
But actually this habit of mind
(profit is just something you
have to have to survive) seems
to me typical of Japanese busi-
ness, and there the motivations
of the boss-man are, very much
so, prestige, status, "face": in
Japan, successful businessmen
are respected, unlike here, and
most Japanese would rather be
respected than rich. Although
this is typical of Japan, it's
by no means unknown elsewhere.

"It would be nice to think,"
says Brian, "that where there is
a potential for a HUGE profit, a
company would be satisfied with
less."

A case study. My employers, ICI,
from the date of their formation
(1926) had a total monopoly on
the manufacture in Britain of
soda ash (washing soda) and were
in the position to charge any
price they liked for it. In
those days, before detergents,
there was a large retail market,
but there was also, and still
is, an even larger industrial
market, mostly for glass making.

Soda ash is cheap to make - it's
really a by-product of chlorine
manufacture, both are products
of electrolysing common salt,
which ICI digs up from its own
salt mines in Cheshire, and the
markets for chlorine were large
and profitable in their own
right.

So did ICI price soda at a mill-
ion pounds a ton?No,they didn't.

Of course, ICI is a public com-
pany, and the profits go to
shareholders, not to the direc-
tors and managers except so far
as they are shareholders them-
selves. But I don't think that
had anything to do with soda ash
pricing policy. They had two
reasons to be restrained:

1. The Belgian producer, Solvay
et Cie, could ship soda ash to
UK if the price was high enough:
the freight cost would be big-
ger than the actual cost of pro-
duction, which would put a fair-
ly high limit on the price, but
still it was a limit.


2. If the market price really
went through the roof,some other
UK enterprise might be tempted
to go into chlorine/ caustic
soda production:rather expensive
for them, but if they did it,
disastrous for ICI not only with
soda but with chlorine as well.



So ICI kept the price of soda
well down, just about high en-
ough to pay for maintaining and
updating the existing plant and
making a modest profit - nothing
for expansion, there wasn't any
prospect of increasing demand,
and nothing for villas in Switz-
erland and the Cayman Islands
for the directors.


Personally I think they were too
cautious, they could have made a
bigger profit and used it to ex-
pand other parts of ICI's busi-
ness. But I ought to emphasize
that I never had any responsi-
bility myself for soda pricing,
all I know about it is from what
I call "company folklore".

        Yours sincerely,



        FRANCIS G MILES

From Harry Hill, ALICANTE, SPAIN





Dear Ron & Brian,

I would like to be enlightened
again on text merge into CLIP
COMPOSER [OUTLET 29]. I have
carried out the instructions
that were in one of the Out-
letters and it was fine but
since then I have forgotten how
to use the text side of it. I
cannot refer to the letter as I
think it is on the "B" side of
OUTLET 83. [lost in disk error]
I have been through all the
disks from 80 to 84.


Also CLIPCOMPOSER will not load
any art clips that are drawn
with ARTIST 2 or the ANIMALS in
OUTLET 35. The only way that I
have managed is to load the clip
then save it with the Multiface
screen save to disk and then
CLIP COMPOSER will load it.

I also use SKETCH from OUTLET 12
which I think is one of the best
yet. I have copied it onto disk
but I am disappointed that I
cannot use the print out or
save; it has to be done through
taping. Have you managed to put
it on disk?If so I would like to
buy a copy from you.
      Thanking you in advance,

            Harry Hill

Brian Cavers to Harry Hill

I can't remember saying anything
recently about "text merge" into
CLIP COMPOSER. The program only
deals in graphic images so any
text needs to be created first -
in whole or in parts - and then
loaded as a screen. For example,
you might use ARTIST 2 or just
the BASIC PRINT (or any of the
special text routines in OUTLET)
to create a screen in BASIC and
then save it as a SCREEN$. For
example, if you save the screen
of giant text from RTCLIP(OUTLET
30) it can be loaded in CLIP
COMPOSER. You then move the box
cursor over a letter and GET it
into a box - it makes sense to
use the same letter, eg, Box A
for letter A, Box B for B.

You then PUT each letter you
want back on the screen you are
creating. For example, you might
load another screen with a clip
art image of a hamster. You then
position the box cursor and use
the PUT feature to put the boxes
H, A, M, S, T, E, and R.

If you want to start on a blank
screen then you might first
create one from BASIC using SAVE
"" SCREEN$ or the MULTIFACE.
Alternatively, you can use GET
then a SHIFT plus a letter key
to lift off different areas or
even the whole screen.

Remember, you can store the RT
CLIP screen and your working
screen separately and do a few
letters at a time.

Remember, text is used in CLIP
COMPOSER just the same as any
image. You have to GET letters
and PUT them where you want to
compose the screen. Like any
creative process, however, it
takes practice. Save your work
regularly using a sequence, eg,
HAMSTER1, HAMSTER2, HAMSTER3 so
if you make a big mistake you
can reload.

I can find no problem loading
screens created by ARTIST 2 or
ANIMAL FORM, indeed the screens
saved from ANIMAL FORM are just
normal SCREEN$ files. You are
probably not saving the files
properly and need to read the
prompts carefully. However, a
Multiface save is fine.


Regarding your converting of the
tape version of SKETCH to +3
disk, the tape save syntax is
identical to the +3 disk syntax
and should work without change.
Simply select tape save and, if
you have loaded SKETCH from +3
disk, it will automatically use
disk for save and load - you
just use the tape option. Do not
use the V to verify option after
however, or it will crash.

As for the print out not working
- well, there is no print out!
Save the screens and print them
from BASIC or any screen dump
utility of your choice.

Please give more details if I've
misunderstood your problems.
                          Brian.

From Kevin Mace, NORTHUMBERLAND

Dear Brian,

I am writing to ask you about
the calendar program, TOP-CAL in
OUTLET 52 by L.G. Baumann. Is it
possible to print part machine
code programs as I am interested
in the working of BASIC programs
and can the programs in OUTLET
themselves be converted to
BASIC?

I notice when I break into the
calendar program, the workings
of BASIC FUNCTION changes when I
move the cursor down the screen
the black line at the bottom of
the screen changes to REM state-
ments and characters.


I have an Amstrad DMP3000 print-
er.I have tried printing the TOP
CAL program but it stops print-
ing after it has just started. I
get and end of file message. The
handbook for the DMP 3000 does
not appear to say how large the
memory is.Is the TOP-CAL program
sending a code that is too long?

The program with the OUTLET rou-
tines at the bottom is 16K bytes
long. Is there a routine to
handle memory functions to the
printer? What are the save rout-
ines for restoring the TOP-CAL
program to BASIC and others like
it?
       Yours faithfully,

             Kevin

Brian Cavers to Kevin Mace

There are several problems asso-
ciated with examining OUTLET
programs in 128K or +3 BASIC.
Most have colour codes or other
control codes embedded in the
listing, machine code routines
embedded in REM lines, and a new
character set. All of these will
upset the 128K editor.To examine
the listing enter SPECTRUM and
switch to 48K. If you are using
a +3 and want to alter a program
and resave it then just enter
RANDOMIZE USR 23354 to get back
to 128K and then RUN 9970 to
erase and resave on the same
disk or RUN 9972 to save a new
copy on a different disk (which
I recommend).


To print out a program listing
on your printer you will usually
need to stay in 128K to access
your printer depending on which
system you have (I am addressing
this reply to all readers, of
course, as a general guide).

You may often need to do it in
parts because some codes in the
listing will stop the printing.
As a general rule type LLIST and
see how far the print out goes.
Look at the last line number
that is printed. Add 1 to that
number and type LLIST XX. For
example, if the first attempt
prints out lines 10 to 50 and
then stops you would enter
LLIST 51. This will normally
start the print from after where
it stopped.

Of course, you may miss a line
or part of a line by this means
but you can later examine the
listing on screen in 48K and
possibly scribble some note on
the print out.

A print out may also terminate
prematurely without any error
message and you may think that
it has printed everything so
check. The only easy way I can
think of to discover what is the
true final line is to type...
LIST 9999 then press ENTER a few
times until you see a line. Note
down the last line number you
see. If it has RANDOMIZE USR...
and ends.. REM NAME CODE then
add 1 and LIST again,eg, if line
9995 then enter LIST 9996.


The reason is that code in REM
lines usually makes any further
lines invisible. However, if you
LIST beyond it using say, LIST
9996 and the screen is clear -
that is,there are no other lines
showing, then that REM line is
the last line.

Incidentally,if you are not used
to 48K BASIC then to LIST just
press the K key instead of typ-
ing L, I, S, T.

When LLISTing you must be in the
"expanded" mode. On the +3 type
FORMAT LPRINT "E" (I think that
is the default at switch on). I
think other 128K machines use
OPEN #3;"P" or OPEN #3;"T" but
check your manual if in doubt.


I haven't got a printer on my +3
so let me guess probable problem
lines in TOP- CAL....

The first 7 or 8 lines have our
CHEZRON address with invisible
line numbers. They may not print
out with the LLIST command. If
so, enter LLIST 9.

Between lines 20 to 30 are three
lines all numbered zero.I'm sure
it will stop here with an error.
When it does, enter LLIST 30.

When you LIST on-screen in 48K
mode you will see colours in the
listing. These should not cause
any problem with printing but
will be filtered out and printed
in black and white.


Line 8850 has coloured graphics.
These should not stop the print
but will probably print as some
unreadable garbage.

The LLISTing should stop at line
9785, possibly 9900, 9994, and
9996. When it does, enter...
LLIST 9786, LLIST 9901, LLIST
9901,and LLIST 9995 as described
earlier. Line 9996 is the last
line in this case.

There is no easy way for you to
list the machine code routines
that are hidden in the REMs. It
is possible to extract them and
save them to disk then load them
into a disassembler such as TOPS
in OUTLET 82 to list but it will
not make any sense to you unless
you know machine code.

You can often work out what the
machine code REM routines do if
you follow the logic of the
BASIC and look at the short name
in the REM. For example, the
print routine has a GO SUB 9785
which has the word COPY in the
REM name - you might guess it
does a copy of the screen to a
printer.Line 9994 has AUTOCHARS,
the thicker, clearer character
set we use in OUTLET while 9996
has the name DUBTEX which is the
double-height text we use.

                        Brian

I will finish on an incident that happened in this area some years ago. A small dealer was selling a TV at less than a large chain store. The large store under its "if you see it cheaper we will refund" did just that.

The firm's interest being in large turnover rather the odd one or two a year from a small business did just that.

There's some justification for it: there are greedy people who run com- panies, milk them of as much cash as they possibly can for as long as they can for their own personal use, and when the sands

have run out liquidate the com- pany (putting all their employ- ees on the dole) and retire to their villa in Switzerland or the Cayman Islands or wherever and lead the life of Riley till they die and go to Hell.

Such people are in a minority: even in England, though I have the impression there are more of them in England (I don't mean Britain) than anywhere else - and I have been around a bit.

Mostly people who run businesses think of profit as a necessary resource, without which the bus- iness can't survive. What do they work for, then, if not per- sonal profit? Some because they

love their work - the craftsman making hand-built furniture, and (I suspect) the Cavers brothers. But actually this habit of mind (profit is just something you have to have to survive) seems to me typical of Japanese busi- ness, and there the motivations of the boss-man are, very much so, prestige, status, "face": in Japan, successful businessmen are respected, unlike here, and most Japanese would rather be respected than rich. Although this is typical of Japan, it's by no means unknown elsewhere.

"It would be nice to think," says Brian, "that where there is a potential for a HUGE profit, a company would be satisfied with less."

A case study. My employers, ICI, from the date of their formation (1926) had a total monopoly on the manufacture in Britain of soda ash (washing soda) and were in the position to charge any price they liked for it. In those days, before detergents, there was a large retail market, but there was also, and still is, an even larger industrial market, mostly for glass making.

Soda ash is cheap to make - it's really a by-product of chlorine manufacture, both are products of electrolysing common salt, which ICI digs up from its own salt mines in Cheshire, and the markets for chlorine were large and profitable in their own right.

So did ICI price soda at a mill- ion pounds a ton?No,they didn't.

Of course, ICI is a public com- pany, and the profits go to shareholders, not to the direc- tors and managers except so far as they are shareholders them- selves. But I don't think that had anything to do with soda ash pricing policy. They had two reasons to be restrained:

1. The Belgian producer, Solvay et Cie, could ship soda ash to UK if the price was high enough: the freight cost would be big- ger than the actual cost of pro- duction, which would put a fair- ly high limit on the price, but still it was a limit.

2. If the market price really went through the roof,some other UK enterprise might be tempted to go into chlorine/ caustic soda production:rather expensive for them, but if they did it, disastrous for ICI not only with soda but with chlorine as well.

So ICI kept the price of soda well down, just about high en- ough to pay for maintaining and updating the existing plant and making a modest profit - nothing for expansion, there wasn't any prospect of increasing demand, and nothing for villas in Switz- erland and the Cayman Islands for the directors.

Personally I think they were too cautious, they could have made a bigger profit and used it to ex- pand other parts of ICI's busi- ness. But I ought to emphasize that I never had any responsi- bility myself for soda pricing, all I know about it is from what I call "company folklore".

Yours sincerely,

There are several problems asso- ciated with examining OUTLET programs in 128K or +3 BASIC. Most have colour codes or other control codes embedded in the listing, machine code routines embedded in REM lines, and a new character set. All of these will upset the 128K editor.To examine the listing enter SPECTRUM and switch to 48K. If you are using a +3 and want to alter a program and resave it then just enter RANDOMIZE USR 23354 to get back to 128K and then RUN 9970 to erase and resave on the same disk or RUN 9972 to save a new copy on a different disk (which I recommend).

To print out a program listing on your printer you will usually need to stay in 128K to access your printer depending on which system you have (I am addressing this reply to all readers, of course, as a general guide).

You may often need to do it in parts because some codes in the listing will stop the printing. As a general rule type LLIST and see how far the print out goes. Look at the last line number that is printed. Add 1 to that number and type LLIST XX. For example, if the first attempt prints out lines 10 to 50 and then stops you would enter LLIST 51. This will normally start the print from after where it stopped.

Of course, you may miss a line or part of a line by this means but you can later examine the listing on screen in 48K and possibly scribble some note on the print out.

A print out may also terminate prematurely without any error message and you may think that it has printed everything so check. The only easy way I can think of to discover what is the true final line is to type... LIST 9999 then press ENTER a few times until you see a line. Note down the last line number you see. If it has RANDOMIZE USR... and ends.. REM NAME CODE then add 1 and LIST again,eg, if line 9995 then enter LIST 9996.

The reason is that code in REM lines usually makes any further lines invisible. However, if you LIST beyond it using say, LIST 9996 and the screen is clear - that is,there are no other lines showing, then that REM line is the last line.

Incidentally,if you are not used to 48K BASIC then to LIST just press the K key instead of typ- ing L, I, S, T.

When LLISTing you must be in the "expanded" mode. On the +3 type FORMAT LPRINT "E" (I think that is the default at switch on). I think other 128K machines use OPEN #3;"P" or OPEN #3;"T" but check your manual if in doubt.

I haven't got a printer on my +3 so let me guess probable problem lines in TOP- CAL....

The first 7 or 8 lines have our CHEZRON address with invisible line numbers. They may not print out with the LLIST command. If so, enter LLIST 9.

Between lines 20 to 30 are three lines all numbered zero.I'm sure it will stop here with an error. When it does, enter LLIST 30.

When you LIST on-screen in 48K mode you will see colours in the listing. These should not cause any problem with printing but will be filtered out and printed in black and white.

Line 8850 has coloured graphics. These should not stop the print but will probably print as some unreadable garbage.

The LLISTing should stop at line 9785, possibly 9900, 9994, and 9996. When it does, enter... LLIST 9786, LLIST 9901, LLIST 9901,and LLIST 9995 as described earlier. Line 9996 is the last line in this case.

There is no easy way for you to list the machine code routines that are hidden in the REMs. It is possible to extract them and save them to disk then load them into a disassembler such as TOPS in OUTLET 82 to list but it will not make any sense to you unless you know machine code.

You can often work out what the machine code REM routines do if you follow the logic of the BASIC and look at the short name in the REM. For example, the print routine has a GO SUB 9785 which has the word COPY in the REM name - you might guess it does a copy of the screen to a printer.Line 9994 has AUTOCHARS, the thicker, clearer character set we use in OUTLET while 9996 has the name DUBTEX which is the double-height text we use.

Brian

С изучением программ OUTLET в среде 128K или +3 BASIC связано несколько проблем. В листинги большинства из них внедрены цветовые коды или другие управляющие символы, подпрограммы в машинных кодах, спрятанные в строках REM, и новый набор символов. Все это сбивает с толку редактор 128K. Чтобы просмотреть листинг, войдите в SPECTRUM и переключитесь в режим 48K. Если вы используете +3 и хотите изменить программу и пересохранить ее, просто введите:

```text
RANDOMIZE USR 23354
```

чтобы вернуться в режим 128K, а затем:

```text
RUN 9970
```

для стирания и повторного сохранения на том же диске, или:

```text
RUN 9972
```

для сохранения новой копии на другом диске (что я и рекомендую).

Чтобы распечатать листинг программы на вашем принтере, вам обычно нужно оставаться в режиме 128K для доступа к принтеру — в зависимости от конфигурации вашей системы (я адресую этот ответ всем читателям как общее руководство).

Зачастую вам придется делать это частями, поскольку некоторые коды в листинге будут прерывать процесс печати. Как правило, введите команду `LLIST` и посмотрите, до какого места дойдет распечатка. Посмотрите на последний напечатанный номер строки. Прибавьте 1 к этому номеру и введите `LLIST XX`. Например, если при первой попытке печатаются строки с 10 по 50, а затем печать останавливается, вам следует ввести:

```text
LLIST 51
```

Обычно это позволяет продолжить печать с того места, где она прервалась.

Конечно, таким способом можно пропустить строку или часть строки, но позже вы сможете изучить листинг на экране в режиме 48K и, возможно, сделать пометки на распечатке от руки.

Печать также может преждевременно завершиться без какого-либо сообщения об ошибке, и вы можете подумать, что напечаталось все, поэтому перепроверяйте. Единственный простой способ узнать реальную последнюю строку, который приходит мне в голову, — это набрать:

```text
LIST 9999
```

а затем нажать несколько раз ENTER, пока не появится строка. Запишите последний номер строки, который увидите. Если там написано `RANDOMIZE USR...` и в конце стоит `REM NAME CODE`, прибавьте 1 и снова дайте команду LIST, например, если это строка 9995, то введите `LIST 9996`.

Причина в том, что код внутри строк REM обычно делает невидимыми любые последующие строки. Однако если вы сделаете LIST дальше нее, используя, скажем, `LIST 9996`, и экран останется чистым — то есть никаких других строк не отображается, значит, эта строка REM действительно последняя.

Кстати, если вы не привыкли к 48K BASIC, то для ввода LIST просто нажмите клавишу K вместо того, чтобы печатать L, I, S, T по буквам.

При выводе по LLIST вы должны находиться в расширенном режиме (expanded mode). На +3 наберите:

```text
FORMAT LPRINT "E"
```

(кажется, он включен по умолчанию при старте). Думаю, другие машины 128K используют:

```text
OPEN #3;"P"
```

или

```text
OPEN #3;"T"
```

но в случае сомнений сверьтесь с вашим руководством.

У меня к +3 принтер не подключен, поэтому позвольте мне угадать вероятные проблемные строки в TOP-CAL...

Первые 7 или 8 строк содержат наш адрес CHEZRON с невидимыми номерами строк. Они могут не распечататься по команде LLIST. В таком случае введите:

```text
LLIST 9
```

Между строками 20 и 30 находятся три строки, у которых номер равен нулю. Я уверен, что печать здесь прервется с ошибкой. Когда это произойдет, введите:

```text
LLIST 30
```

Когда вы сделаете LIST на экране в режиме 48K, то увидите цвета в листинге. Они не должны вызывать никаких проблем с печатью — они будут отфильтрованы и напечатаны в черно-белом виде.

В строке 8850 содержится цветная графика. Она не должна останавливать печать, но, скорее всего, распечатается в виде нечитаемого мусора.

Команда LLIST должна остановиться на строке 9785, возможно на 9900, 9994 и 9996. Когда это случится, вводите:

```text
LLIST 9786
LLIST 9901
LLIST 9901
LLIST 9995
```

как было описано ранее. Строка 9996 в данном случае является последней.

У вас нет простого способа распечатать подпрограммы в машинных кодах, скрытые в операторах REM. Их можно извлечь и сохранить на диск, а затем загрузить в дизассемблер, такой как TOPS из OUTLET 82, чтобы получить листинг, но в этом не будет никакого смысла, если вы не знаете машинный код.

Часто можно понять, что делают подпрограммы в машинных кодах, находящиеся в строках REM, если проследить логику бейсика и взглянуть на краткое название в REM. Например, в процедуре печати есть GO SUB 9785, содержащий слово COPY в названии REM — можно догадаться, что она делает копию экрана на принтер. В строке 9994 находится AUTOCHARS — более жирный и чёткий набор символов, который мы используем в OUTLET, а в строке 9996 — DUBTEX, то есть используемый нами текст двойной высоты.
